Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Thousands of people marched in central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in the country after the end of the year. Thousands staged a mass march through Baghdad, Iraq, on Saturday to protest a planned U.S.-Iraq security deal. The political party of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr called for the rally. At one point, several speakers at a podium addressed the mass of people, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal. "End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!" one speaker shouted in English. Hazem al-Araji, a senior al-Sadr aide, told protesters their voices would be heard in America. "Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his 'Black House' -- in which you shouted out, 'No, no, America!'" he said.  Watch protesters wave flags, swarm street » . "This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!" al-Araji exclaimed. Protesters clogged several streets in the capital, waving Iraqi flags and kicking up dust. The demonstration, the largest in Baghdad in several months, was largely peaceful. Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said in Washington on Thursday a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq had "been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators" and was being reviewed by the two governments. A U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq expires December 31, and U.S. officials are examining "contingencies" in case the Iraqi government is unable to sell the status-of-forces deal to the country's various factions, a senior Bush administration official said this week. The same official said negotiations on the pact had finished and the text was final. The official said the "final" draft calls for U.S. troops to be out of Iraqi cities by June 2009 and out of Iraq by the end of 2011 unless the Iraqis ask the United States to stay. The U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said negotiators had also "reached a compromise" on the issue of U.S. troops remaining immune from Iraqi law -- an issue that was a major hurdle in the talks. Baghdad has sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit grave mistakes in the course of their duties. The United States has insisted its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Thousands of demonstrators marched through central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the American military presence in the country beyond the end of the year. The mass demonstration, organized at the behest of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr's political party, wound through the streets of the capital in opposition to the planned deal.

At various points during the rally, speakers addressed the crowd from a podium, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal. "End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!" one speaker shouted in English.

Hazem al-Araji, a senior aide to al-Sadr, assured protesters that their message would resonate across the Atlantic. "Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his 'Black House' -- in which you shouted out, 'No, no, America!'" he declared.

"This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!" al-Araji continued.

Protesters filled several thoroughfares in the capital, waving Iraqi flags amid clouds of dust. The demonstration, the largest witnessed in Baghdad in several months, remained largely peaceful throughout.

In Washington on Thursday, Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell confirmed that a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the continued U.S. troop presence in Iraq had "been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators" and was currently under review by both governments.

A United Nations mandate sanctioning the U.S. military presence in Iraq is set to expire on December 31, and American officials are reportedly weighing contingency plans should the Iraqi government struggle to secure support for the agreement among the country's various political factions, according to a senior Bush administration official who spoke this week. The same official indicated that negotiations on the pact had concluded and that the text was now final.

According to this official, the finalized draft stipulates that U.S. forces will withdraw from Iraqi cities by June 2009 and depart the country entirely by the end of 2011, unless Iraqi authorities request an extended American presence.

Speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the discussions, the official noted that negotiators had also reached a compromise on the contentious issue of legal immunity for U.S. troops under Iraqi law—a matter that had posed a significant obstacle throughout the talks. Baghdad had sought authority to arrest and prosecute American personnel accused of crimes unrelated to official military duties, as well as jurisdiction over troops and contractors responsible for serious misconduct in the course of their work. The United States, for its part, had insisted that its troops and contractors retain immunity from Iraqi legal jurisdiction.

CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.

# Thousands March in Baghdad Against U.S. Security Pact

BAGHDAD — Tens of thousands of Iraqis flooded the streets of central Baghdad on Saturday in one of the largest demonstrations the capital has witnessed in months, answering a call from followers of the influential Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr to protest the continued American military presence in Iraq and a controversial security agreement that would extend it beyond the end of this year.

Waving Iraqi flags and carrying banners denouncing the "occupation," protesters marched from several staging points toward the center of the city, chanting slogans that called for the immediate withdrawal of U.S. forces and condemned what they described as an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty. Many demonstrators wore white burial shrouds, a symbolic gesture signaling their willingness to die resisting the American presence, while others carried portraits of al-Sadr and effigies representing the United States.

The demonstration, organized and mobilized largely through al-Sadr's political and social networks, remained largely peaceful, with Iraqi security forces monitoring the crowds but reporting no major incidents of violence. The scale of the turnout was seen as a significant show of force by the Sadrist movement, which has consistently opposed the presence of American troops since the 2003 invasion and has positioned itself as a leading voice against the proposed security arrangement.

At issue is a draft agreement being negotiated between American and Iraqi officials that would govern the legal status of U.S. forces in Iraq after December 31, when the United Nations mandate authorizing their presence is set to expire. The proposed pact, details of which have been debated intensely in Iraqi political circles, would allow American troops to remain in the country for a specified period beyond this year, subject to certain conditions and timelines for eventual withdrawal.

Saturday's protest reflects deepening unease among segments of the Iraqi public and political class over the terms of the deal, even as negotiators from both governments work to finalize its language in the coming weeks. Critics, including al-Sadr's followers, argue that the agreement fails to set a firm and immediate timetable for the departure of foreign forces and instead risks legitimizing a prolonged American military footprint in the country.

Iraqi government officials, who have been engaged in painstaking talks with their American counterparts, have defended the negotiating process, saying that any final agreement will be presented to parliament for approval and will include safeguards protecting Iraqi sovereignty. Nonetheless, the size and intensity of Saturday's demonstration signal that opposition to the pact extends beyond al-Sadr's base and taps into broader nationalist sentiment among ordinary Iraqis who have grown weary of the prolonged foreign military presence.

With the December 31 deadline approaching and the U.N. mandate set to lapse, pressure is mounting on both Washington and Baghdad to reach a resolution that can satisfy security needs while addressing the political sensitivities laid bare by Saturday's mass mobilization. The demonstration serves as a pointed reminder to negotiators on both sides that any final agreement will face intense scrutiny — and potentially significant public resistance — as it moves toward ratification.

# Baghdad: A City at the Crossroads of History and Modern Media

Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, stands as one of the most historically significant cities in the Middle East. Founded in the 8th century, it once served as the intellectual and cultural capital of the Islamic world during the Abbasid Caliphate, home to the legendary House of Wisdom where scholars translated and preserved classical knowledge. Today, Baghdad remains Iraq's largest city and its political, economic, and cultural center, situated along the historic Tigris River.

In recent decades, Baghdad has frequently appeared in international headlines, particularly through the lens of major news organizations like CNN. Since the early 1990s, CNN has played a pivotal role in shaping global perceptions of the city, beginning with its groundbreaking live coverage of the Gulf War in 1991. Correspondents reporting from Baghdad hotel rooms as airstrikes lit up the night sky became iconic images that demonstrated the power of 24-hour news broadcasting.

This relationship between CNN and Baghdad continued through subsequent conflicts, including the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when the network provided extensive coverage of the war's progression, the fall of Saddam Hussein's government, and the challenging years of reconstruction and insurgency that followed. CNN's Baghdad bureau became one of the network's most important international outposts, staffed by journalists who reported on everything from political developments to the daily struggles of ordinary Iraqi citizens.

Beyond conflict coverage, CNN and other international media outlets have also documented Baghdad's efforts at rebuilding and modernization, capturing stories of resilience among its residents. The city's ancient markets, universities, and neighborhoods have been portrayed alongside images of destruction and recovery, offering global audiences a more complete picture of a metropolis navigating profound challenges.

The relationship between Baghdad and international news coverage illustrates broader themes about how media shapes understanding of conflict zones, the responsibilities of journalists reporting from dangerous environments, and the ongoing efforts to tell nuanced stories about places often reduced to symbols of war in public consciousness. As Iraq continues its path toward stability, Baghdad remains a city whose story continues to be told, in part, through the lens of international news networks working to bring its reality to audiences worldwide.

# Thousands Rally in Baghdad Against U.S.-Iraq Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Tens of thousands of demonstrators flooded the streets of Baghdad on Friday in one of the largest organized protests since the fall of Saddam Hussein, voicing fierce opposition to the proposed security agreement between the United States and Iraq that would govern the future presence of American troops in the country.

The protest, organized largely by followers of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, drew massive crowds from Sadr City and other Baghdad neighborhoods, with demonstrators marching through the capital chanting slogans against what they characterize as an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty.

Protesters carried banners reading "No, No to the Agreement" and "Occupation Out Now," while others burned American flags in scenes reminiscent of earlier waves of anti-occupation sentiment that swept the country in the years following the 2003 invasion.

"This agreement is nothing more than an attempt to legalize the occupation of Iraq for years to come," said Sadrist parliamentary bloc spokesman Liwaa Sumaisim, addressing the crowd from a stage erected near the demonstration's endpoint. "We reject any pact that keeps foreign troops on our soil beyond what our people demand."

The security agreement, which has been the subject of tense negotiations between Washington and Baghdad, would establish a legal framework for U.S. forces operating in Iraq after the expiration of the United Nations mandate. Critics within the Sadrist movement argue that draft versions of the agreement fail to set a firm timetable for full American withdrawal and grant U.S. forces broad legal immunities they say violate Iraqi sovereignty.

"We say to the Iraqi government: you do not have the right to sign away our sovereignty," Sheikh Abdul Hadi al-Mohammedawi, a senior Sadrist cleric, told the assembled crowd through a loudspeaker system. "The Iraqi people did not elect this government to auction off our independence to foreign powers."

Organizers said the demonstration was intended to send an unambiguous message to Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government as negotiations with U.S. officials continue behind closed doors.

Iraqi security forces maintained a heavy but largely restrained presence throughout the protest, with checkpoints established around the demonstration route. There were no immediate reports of violence, though the scale of the gathering underscored the depth of public unease surrounding the pact.

The Sadrist movement, which maintains both a political bloc in the Iraqi parliament and the Mahdi Army militia, has consistently positioned itself as the leading voice of opposition to the U.S. military presence, even as other Iraqi political blocs have shown more willingness to negotiate terms with Washington.

"Muqtada al-Sadr has instructed his followers that this is a red line," said Salah al-Obeidi, a spokesman for the cleric's office in Najaf. "The Iraqi people have suffered enough. They will not accept a document that extends foreign military jurisdiction over their land indefinitely."

U.S. and Iraqi officials have continued negotiations despite the public backlash, with American officials expressing hope that a finalized agreement could be reached before the U.N. mandate's expiration. However, Friday's demonstration illustrates the significant domestic political pressure facing Iraqi negotiators as they attempt to balance security concerns with growing public demands for full sovereignty.

Similar smaller protests were reported in Basra, Kut, and other predominantly Shiite areas in the south, suggesting the demonstration in Baghdad was part of a coordinated nationwide campaign by Sadrist organizers to pressure the government ahead of a parliamentary vote on the agreement's final terms.

*This is a developing story.*

# Thousands Rally in Baghdad as Sadr Followers Denounce U.S.-Iraq Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Tens of thousands of demonstrators flooded the streets of Baghdad's Sadr City district and other Shiite strongholds this week, answering a call from followers of cleric Muqtada al-Sadr to protest a proposed security agreement that would govern the future presence of American troops in Iraq.

Chanting "No, no to the occupation!" and waving Iraqi flags alongside banners bearing images of al-Sadr, protesters marched through the capital in one of the largest coordinated demonstrations Iraq has seen since the height of sectarian violence in 2006 and 2007. Organizers said the crowds numbered in the tens of thousands, with similar smaller protests reported in Basra, Kut, and other cities with strong Sadrist followings.

## Opposition to the Pact

At the center of the demonstrations is the status-of-forces agreement (SOFA) being negotiated between Baghdad and Washington, which would replace the United Nations mandate authorizing the presence of foreign troops in Iraq, set to expire at the end of the year. The draft agreement reportedly includes a timeline for the withdrawal of American combat forces from Iraqi cities by mid-2009 and a full withdrawal by the end of 2011.

Despite these provisions, Sadrist leaders have rejected the agreement outright, characterizing it as a continuation of foreign occupation dressed in diplomatic language. Speaking to supporters, representatives of al-Sadr's movement argued that any agreement permitting U.S. forces to remain on Iraqi soil — even temporarily — represents an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty.

"This agreement is nothing but a new mask for the occupation," one Sadrist official told the crowd in Sadr City, echoing sentiments repeated at rallies across the capital. "We will not accept the presence of foreign troops on our land, no matter what paper they sign."

## A Show of Political Strength

The demonstrations also served as a visible display of the Sadrist movement's continued influence in Iraqi politics, despite the cleric's own relative absence from the public eye — al-Sadr has spent much of the past year in Iran, reportedly furthering his religious studies. Analysts say the protests were as much about reasserting the movement's relevance ahead of expected provincial elections as they were about the SOFA itself.

Protesters carried posters denouncing Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government for engaging in negotiations with Washington, accusing his administration of capitulating to American pressure. Some marchers called for the dissolution of parliament if the agreement were ratified without further amendments.

Security was tight throughout Baghdad during the demonstrations, with Iraqi army and police units deployed along major routes into Sadr City, though the protests themselves remained largely peaceful.

## Government Response

Iraqi officials have sought to downplay the demonstrations while defending the ongoing negotiations. Government spokesmen have emphasized that the draft agreement includes explicit language on troop withdrawal timelines and restrictions on U.S. military operations, arguing that it represents a step toward reclaiming full Iraqi sovereignty rather than undermining it.

Nonetheless, the scale of the Sadrist protests underscores the deep divisions within Iraqi society over the terms of the American military presence, more than five years after the 2003 invasion. Sunni and Kurdish political blocs have offered more measured responses to the draft pact, while some hardline Shiite factions beyond the Sadrists have echoed concerns about the agreement's implications for Iraqi sovereignty.

## What Comes Next

With the U.N. mandate set to expire on December 31, pressure is mounting on Iraqi lawmakers to reach a final decision. The Iraqi parliament is expected to debate the agreement in the coming weeks, and Sadrist lawmakers have vowed to campaign vigorously against its ratification.

Whether the demonstrations will be enough to derail the agreement remains uncertain, but they have unmistakably signaled that opposition to the American military presence — and to the political process shaping its future — remains a potent force in Iraqi public life.

*This report reflects developments as of late 2008, during ongoing negotiations over the U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement.*

# Thousands Rally in Baghdad, Demanding U.S. Troop Withdrawal Timeline

**BAGHDAD** — Tens of thousands of demonstrators gathered in central Baghdad on [day], marching from several neighborhoods to converge near the Green Zone in one of the largest public protests since [reference period], demanding a clear timetable for the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq.

Organizers, including supporters of prominent political and religious factions, said the demonstration was intended to pressure both the Iraqi government and Washington to set firm benchmarks for ending the U.S. military presence. Protesters carried Iraqi flags, banners reading "Occupation Out Now," and portraits of religious leaders as they chanted slogans calling for sovereignty and an end to what they described as prolonged foreign military control.

Iraqi security forces, deployed in large numbers along the protest route, reported no major clashes, though officials said several smaller scuffles were contained without serious injury. Traffic was halted across large parts of the capital for much of the day.

## Political Reaction in Baghdad

Iraqi government spokespeople sought to strike a balance between acknowledging public frustration and reaffirming security cooperation with U.S.-led coalition forces. A senior official said the government "understands the sentiment of the Iraqi people" but stressed that any withdrawal must be "conditions-based" to avoid destabilizing recent security gains.

## Pentagon Response

At a briefing in Washington, a Pentagon spokesperson said U.S. commanders continue to assess conditions on the ground and reiterated that troop levels would be adjusted "based on the recommendations of commanders, not on a fixed calendar."

"We remain committed to a responsible transition of security responsibilities to Iraqi forces," the spokesperson said. "That transition will be based on conditions, not arbitrary deadlines that could put at risk the progress our forces and our Iraqi partners have made."

Defense officials declined to comment on specific troop numbers or projected withdrawal dates, noting that any adjustments would be announced following consultations with the Iraqi government and regional military commanders.

## White House Position

A White House spokesperson, addressing the Baghdad demonstration during a press briefing, said the administration respected the right of Iraqis to protest peacefully but rejected calls for an immediate or fixed withdrawal timeline.

"The president has been clear that a hasty withdrawal would undermine the sacrifices made by our troops and the Iraqi people," the spokesperson said. "We will continue to work closely with the Iraqi government on a transition that reflects conditions on the ground."

Administration officials pointed to ongoing negotiations over a bilateral security agreement between Washington and Baghdad, which they said would eventually include provisions addressing the future presence of U.S. forces.

## Reaction from Lawmakers

The protest drew renewed attention on Capitol Hill, where members of Congress remain divided over Iraq policy. Some lawmakers renewed calls for legislation setting withdrawal benchmarks, while others echoed the administration's position that conditions on the ground should dictate any drawdown.

## Looking Ahead

Iraqi officials said talks over the security agreement governing the long-term U.S. military role are expected to continue in the coming weeks. Protest organizers vowed to continue demonstrations until a formal timeline is established, setting the stage for continued tension between public sentiment in Iraq and the cautious, conditions-based approach favored by Washington.

*(Additional reporting contributed by correspondents in Washington.)*

# Iraqi Protesters Demand U.S. Troop Withdrawal Ahead of UN Mandate Deadline

Thousands of Iraqi demonstrators took to the streets in Baghdad and other cities this week, calling for the complete withdrawal of American forces as the December 31 deadline for the United Nations mandate governing the U.S. military presence in Iraq approaches.

## Background on the UN Mandate

The UN Security Council resolution authorizing foreign troop operations in Iraq has served as the legal framework for the U.S. military presence since the initial invasion. With the mandate set to expire at the end of the year, Iraqi and American officials have been negotiating a bilateral security agreement to replace it—a process that has become increasingly contentious both in Baghdad and Washington.

## Protesters' Demands

Demonstrators, organized in part by followers of Shiite cleric Moqtada al-Sadr and other political factions, marched through central Baghdad chanting slogans against the continued American troop presence. Protest organizers said their central grievance is opposition to any agreement that would extend the U.S. military's stay in Iraq beyond the current mandate's expiration.

"We reject any pact that keeps foreign occupation forces on Iraqi soil," one protest organizer told reporters, echoing sentiments expressed at rallies across the capital.

## Sticking Points in Negotiations

At the heart of the dispute is the question of legal immunity for U.S. soldiers and contractors operating in Iraq. American negotiators have pushed for provisions that would shield U.S. personnel from prosecution under Iraqi law, arguing such protections are standard in agreements governing foreign military deployments.

Iraqi lawmakers and public figures have pushed back, with many arguing that granting blanket immunity would infringe on Iraqi sovereignty and accountability, particularly given the toll of the war on Iraqi civilians. Other contested issues reportedly include the duration of any new agreement, the scope of U.S. military operations permitted on Iraqi soil, and control over detention of prisoners held by American forces.

## Political Pressure

The negotiations have placed pressure on Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government, which must balance relations with Washington against a domestic political climate increasingly wary of prolonged foreign military involvement. Sunni, Shiite, and Kurdish blocs in parliament have all voiced concerns over various elements of the proposed pact, though for differing reasons.

U.S. officials have maintained that failure to reach an agreement before the deadline could create legal ambiguity for troops remaining in the country, while Iraqi officials have signaled they may seek a short-term extension of the UN mandate if a comprehensive deal cannot be finalized in time.

As talks continue, further demonstrations are expected in the coming weeks, with organizers vowing to keep pressure on both governments ahead of the year-end deadline.
